overview: Montserrat’s history includes Indigenous beadmaking, plantation labour, community schooling and music. Volcanic eruptions forced major changes after 1995, but the island’s society continued. This card connects discoveries and everyday life across the two map records for the same island.

periods.title: Plantation colonial society
periods.summary: English settlement began in 1632. French invasions interrupted colonial control, including occupation from 1782 to 1784. Plantation slavery shaped island life.

periods.title: Abolition followed by apprenticeship
periods.summary: Abolition in 1834 led to compulsory apprenticeship rather than immediate freedom from coerced labour.

periods.title: Emancipation and changing livelihoods
periods.summary: Apprenticeship ended in 1838. Communities developed schools while the colonial economy shifted toward citrus limes and, later, cotton.

periods.title: Eruption, displacement and rebuilding
periods.summary: Soufrière Hills began erupting in July 1995. Plymouth’s final evacuation came in April 1996; destructive flows reached the town in 1997.

periods.title: Continuing territory under a new constitution
periods.summary: The 2010 Constitution Order took effect in September 2011. Montserrat remained a British Overseas Territory.

sections.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage

items.text: At precolonial Trants, stone and shell beads survive alongside evidence of unfinished production. David Watters’s research identified manufacturing stages showing that island craftspeople worked imported raw materials. Other beads may have arrived already finished. A necklace can therefore reveal both skilled local work and connections across the sea; it does not by itself identify the wearer’s rank.

At Little Bay’s eighteenth-century cattle mill, archaeologists exposed a masonry channel in 2006. It carried pressed cane juice through the mill wall toward the boiling house, where the juice became sugar. This surviving connection helps reconstruct the sequence of plantation work. The archive also reports missing field records, so later sediment and pottery cannot simply be treated as the mill’s original floor.

In Area 2 of Little Bay’s workers’ village, a ditch cut around a house platform appears to have diverted rainwater from the home. Stone alignments also suggested steps and supports. These modest traces illuminate household care under slavery. Erosion and later land use damaged the site, making a complete reconstruction of each home impossible.

The workers’ village also yielded fragments of handmade earthenware associated with cooking, eating and storing water. Some vessel identifications remain tentative because the pieces are small. Imported ceramics and bottle glass occur too. A broken pot is useful evidence, but it cannot tell us every ingredient in the family’s supper.

After apprenticeship ended, emancipated Montserratians founded primary schools for their children. Brown University’s project chronology records seventeen schools in 1840, compared with one in 1838. Archaeologists excavated a schoolhouse on Potato Hill, where toys were among the finds. Education became part of building life after slavery.

In July 2012, seven Montserrat Secondary School pupils aged thirteen to sixteen joined a three-week archaeology programme. They excavated, washed and labelled finds, and then led public tours. Lessons included reading old documents critically. Here, learning history meant doing some of the investigating and explaining it to the adults.

Goat water belongs in a dinner bowl: despite the name, it is a meat stew. The tourism authority describes it as a communal dish at weddings, christenings, parties and funerals, and a favourite Friday lunch. Cooking over a wood fire contributes flavour. The shared meal brings people together at very different moments in family life.

AIR Montserrat opened in 1979 and brought recording technology and musicians to the island. Its studio history lists work by local artist Arrow as well as Dire Straits, the Police and other visiting performers. Hurricane Hugo damaged the building and equipment in 1989, ending this studio’s operation years before the volcano crisis.

sections.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community

items.text: The eruption that began on 18 July 1995 changed where people could live and work. Plymouth was evacuated repeatedly before the final evacuation in April 1996. Pyroclastic currents, fast-moving mixtures of volcanic material and gas, reached the town in 1997. Losing a capital and homes was a human disaster, not a disappearance of Montserratian people or identity.

Even the scientists had to move. The observatory began in temporary premises in Plymouth, relocated as evacuation zones expanded, and eventually operated from Mongo Hill, where staff could not actually see the volcano. A purpose-built facility followed in 2003. Monitoring depended on instruments and teamwork as well as watching the mountain.

Volcano monitoring combines several kinds of clues. Instruments record earthquakes, ground movement and gas emissions; solar-powered remote stations can send measurements back to the observatory. These observations help scientists assess changing conditions. Montserrat’s scientific achievement includes sustained measurement and communication, rather than a machine that predicts an eruption with certainty.

At the National Museum in Little Bay, visitors can learn about precolonial life and more recent history, and try playable musical instruments. Preserving culture can involve making a sound yourself as well as looking at an old object. The museum represents continuing community work in the island’s north.

ending.text: Montserrat continues as a British Overseas Territory. Plymouth’s evacuation and destruction changed where people lived, while cultural and scientific institutions continued elsewhere. The constitution introduced in 2011 did not grant independence. The map’s endpoints are not the end of Montserratian society.
